probes.question: How many colours are enough to colour any map so neighbouring regions differ?

image.alt: Flat illustration of a map of nine regions filled with four colours (teal, orange, navy and gold), with no two neighbouring regions sharing a colour.

body.claim: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so that no two neighbouring regions share a colour.
body.why: Mathematicians have suspected this since 1852, when Francis Guthrie noticed it while colouring a map of English counties. It was finally proved in 1976, and the proof was one of the first major ones to rely on a computer checking over a thousand cases. Some mathematicians were uneasy that no human could check it all by hand.
